# What is population structure?

## Population structure in one slide

- Individuals form **groups** with **different allele frequencies**
- Causes: limited gene flow (distance, barriers), drift, selection, and the **breeder's choice of crosses**
- Humans: genetic ancestry **follows geography**, from continents (Rosenberg et al. 2002) down to countries in Europe (Novembre et al. 2008)

<!-- TODO: incluir aqui o exemplo do Rodrigo -->

::: notes
Population structure means that genotypes are not spread at random: there are
groups of individuals that share allele frequencies more with each other than
with the rest. It appears whenever mating is not random: geographic distance,
physical barriers, genetic drift in small groups, selection and, in plants
and animals, the breeder deciding who is crossed with whom. In humans, the
classic examples are Rosenberg et al. (2002), where STRUCTURE splits 52
worldwide populations into continental groups, and Novembre et al. (2008),
where a PCA of European genotypes reproduces the map of Europe.
:::

## Human example: genes mirror geography

```{r}
#| label: g-humanos
#| fig-height: 6
set.seed(2008)
# Simulação: indivíduos numa grade de "regiões"; a frequência de cada SNP
# muda suavemente com a posição (isolamento por distância)
regioes <- CJ(lon = 1:8, lat = 1:5)
n_snp <- 400
a <- rnorm(n_snp, 0, 0.35); b <- rnorm(n_snp, 0, 0.35); c0 <- rnorm(n_snp, 0, 1)
ind <- regioes[rep(seq_len(.N), each = 6)]
G <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(ind)), function(i)
  rbinom(n_snp, 2, plogis(a * (ind$lon[i] - 4.5) + b * (ind$lat[i] - 3) + c0))))
pc <- prcomp(G)$x
# o sinal dos PCs é arbitrário: alinha com a orientação do mapa
ind[, `:=`(PC1 = pc[, 1] * sign(cor(pc[, 1], lon)),
           PC2 = pc[, 2] * sign(cor(pc[, 2], lat)))]
ind[, cor := hcl(h = 15 + (lon - 1) * 40, c = 70, l = 30 + lat * 9)]
ind[, `:=`(xj = lon + runif(.N, -0.3, 0.3), yj = lat + runif(.N, -0.3, 0.3))]
(ggplot(ind, aes(xj, yj, colour = I(cor))) +
   geom_point(size = 3.5) + coord_equal() + tema_vazio +
   labs(title = "Where people live")) +
  (ggplot(ind, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = I(cor))) +
     geom_point(size = 3.5) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) +
     labs(title = "PCA of their genotypes"))
```

::: destaque
Simulated, as in Novembre et al. 2008: the PCA redraws the map
:::

::: notes
This is a simulation inspired by Novembre et al. (2008). People live on a
map; each colour is a region. Allele frequencies change gradually with
distance, because people tend to have children with neighbours. A PCA of the
genotypes alone, without any information on location, places the individuals
in the same arrangement as the map. Novembre et al. found exactly this with
real data from about 1,400 Europeans.
:::

## Populations do not mate at random

```{r}
#| label: g-panmixia
#| fig-height: 6.4
n <- 160
pan <- data.table(x = runif(n, -1, 1), y = runif(n, -1, 1),
                  alelo = sample(c("A", "a"), n, TRUE), cenario = "Panmixia")
est <- rbind(
  data.table(x = runif(n / 2, -1, -0.15), y = runif(n / 2, -1, 1),
             alelo = sample(c("A", "a"), n / 2, TRUE, c(0.85, 0.15))),
  data.table(x = runif(n / 2, 0.15, 1), y = runif(n / 2, -1, 1),
             alelo = sample(c("A", "a"), n / 2, TRUE, c(0.15, 0.85)))
)[, cenario := "Structured"]
d <- rbind(pan, est)[, cenario := factor(cenario, c("Panmixia", "Structured"))]

ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = alelo)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_vline(data = data.table(cenario = factor("Structured",
                                                levels(d$cenario)), x = 0),
             aes(xintercept = x), linewidth = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ cenario) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cor_alelo, name = "allele") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.2)))
```

::: destaque
Subpopulations → different allele frequencies
:::

::: notes
In a panmictic population, any individual can mate with any other, and allele
frequencies are the same everywhere. When there are barriers (geography,
selection, a breeder choosing the crosses), each subpopulation drifts to its
own frequencies. That is structure: genotypes are not distributed at random.
:::

## Why does it matter?

```{r}
#| label: g-importancia
#| fig-height: 5.8
# Grão de milho desenhado como uma superelipse; o dent tem a depressão no topo
grao <- function(tipo, cx) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 400)
  x <- 0.42 * sign(cos(t)) * abs(cos(t))^0.7
  y <- 0.55 * sign(sin(t)) * abs(sin(t))^0.9
  if (tipo == "dent") {
    x <- x * 1.1
    y <- ifelse(y > 0, y - 0.18 * exp(-(x / 0.18)^2) * (y / 0.55), y)
  } else {
    y <- y * 0.92
  }
  data.table(x = x + cx, y = y, tipo = tipo)
}
graos <- rbind(grao("dent", 0), grao("flint", 1.3))
p_melhoramento <- ggplot(graos, aes(x, y, group = tipo, fill = tipo)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "grey25", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = c(0, 1.3), y = -0.8, label = c("dent", "flint"),
           size = 8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(dent = "#F2C94C", flint = "#E67E22"),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(clip = "off") + tema_vazio +
  labs(title = "Breeding", subtitle = "heterotic groups")

# Vicariância: um rio separa uma população em duas
v <- rbind(data.table(x = runif(70, -1, -0.15), y = runif(70, -1, 1), pop = "a"),
           data.table(x = runif(70, 0.15, 1), y = runif(70, -1, 1), pop = "b"))
rio <- data.table(y = seq(-1.1, 1.1, length.out = 100))[, x := 0.07 * sin(y * 9)]
p_biologia <- ggplot(v, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(data = rio, colour = "#4A90D9", linewidth = 5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = pop), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(a = "#7B3294", b = "#008837"), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() + tema_vazio +
  labs(title = "Biology", subtitle = "vicariance → speciation")

# Manhattan plot simulado: picos que podem ser só estrutura
m <- data.table(chr = rep(1:10, each = 300))[, pos := seq_len(.N), by = chr]
m[, p := -log10(runif(.N))]
m[chr %in% c(2, 5, 8), p := p + 9 * exp(-((pos - 150) / 12)^2)]
m[, x := (chr - 1) * 330 + pos]
p_gwas <- ggplot(m, aes(x, p, colour = factor(chr %% 2))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 7.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey30", "grey65"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "chromosome", y = "−log10 p", title = "GWAS",
       subtitle = "spurious peaks") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey30"))

p_melhoramento + p_biologia + p_gwas
```

::: notes
Three reasons. Breeding: maize hybrids come from crossing two heterotic
groups (here, dent and flint kernels); knowing which group a line belongs to
tells us what to cross it with. Biology: when a barrier (a river, a mountain)
splits a population, the two halves diverge, and that can lead to
speciation (vicariance); structure records this history. GWAS: in
association studies, ignoring structure produces peaks that are not real
(false positives), as the next slide shows.
:::

## Spurious association: type I error

```{r}
#| label: g-associacao-falsa
#| fig-height: 6.4
n <- 200
d <- rbind(
  data.table(pop = "Population 1", snp = rbinom(n, 2, 0.8),
             altura = rnorm(n, 2.4, 0.12)),
  data.table(pop = "Population 2", snp = rbinom(n, 2, 0.2),
             altura = rnorm(n, 2.0, 0.12))
)
ggplot(d, aes(snp, altura)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = pop), width = 0.15, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = pop), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#7B3294", "#008837"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:2, labels = c("aa", "Aa", "AA")) +
  labs(x = "SNP genotype", y = "plant height (m)")
```

::: destaque
The SNP has no effect: the difference comes from the population
:::

::: notes
Simulation: the SNP does not affect height. Population 1 is taller and carries
more of allele A. Pooling everything (black line), allele A seems to increase
height. Within each population (dashed lines), there is no effect at all. This
is why GWAS corrects for structure (STRUCTURE's Q matrix or PCs as
covariates).
:::

# The data: CornFed panels

## Dent × Flint: two heterotic groups

```{r}
#| label: g-heterose
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
diagrama(
  data.table(id = c("D", "F", "H"), x = c(0, 0, 4.2), y = c(1, -1, 0),
             rotulo = c("Dent\nCorn Belt (USA)\nB73, Mo17",
                        "Flint\nEurope\nearly, cold-tolerant",
                        "Hybrid\nheterosis"),
             cor = c(cor_pool[["Dent"]], cor_pool[["Flint"]], "#FF7F00")),
  data.table(de = c("D", "F"), para = c("H", "H")),
  largura = 3.4, altura = 1.6)
```

::: notes
The two groups have been kept apart for decades to maximise heterosis in the
dent × flint hybrid. We expect this to be the strongest split in the data
(K = 2).
:::

## One central line × 10 to 12 founders

```{r}
#| label: g-desenho
#| fig-height: 6.6
desenho <- data.table(
  pool = rep(c("Dent", "Flint"), c(11, 13)),
  central = rep(c("F353", "UH007"), c(11, 13)),
  familia = c("CFD01", "CFD02", "CFD03", "CFD04", "CFD05", "CFD06", "CFD07",
              "CFD09", "CFD10", "CFD11", "CFD12",
              "CFF01", "CFF02", "CFF03", "CFF04", "CFF05", "CFF06", "CFF07",
              "CFF08", "CFF09", "CFF10", "CFF12", "CFF13", "CFF15"),
  fundadora = c("UH007", "B73", "D06", "D09", "EC169", "F252", "F618", "Mo17",
                "UH250", "UH304", "W117",
                "F353", "B73", "D152", "EC49A", "EP44", "EZ5", "F03802", "F2",
                "F283", "F64", "UH006", "UH009", "DK105")
)
desenho[, ang := 2 * pi * (seq_len(.N) - 1) / .N, by = pool]
desenho[, `:=`(x = cos(ang), y = sin(ang))]
# fundadora do outro pool: são as famílias "misturadas"
desenho[, outro_pool := familia %in% c("CFD01", "CFF01", "CFF02")]
centros <- unique(desenho[, .(pool, central)])

ggplot(desenho) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y, colour = outro_pool),
               linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_label(aes(x * 1.18, y * 1.18, label = fundadora, colour = outro_pool),
             size = 6, label.size = 0) +
  geom_label(data = centros, aes(0, 0, label = central, fill = pool),
             colour = "white", size = 8, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ pool) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey35", `TRUE` = "#FF7F00"),
                      labels = c("founder from the same pool",
                                 "founder from the other pool"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cor_pool, guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(clip = "off") +
  theme_void(base_size = 24) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.2)))
```

::: notes
Each family comes from crossing the pool's central line (F353 in dent, UH007
in flint) with one founder. So the families within a pool are half-sibs.
Three families have parents from both pools (orange): CFD01 and CFF01 are the
cross between the two central lines, and CFF02 has B73 (dent) as founder.
These are our controls: they should show ~50% of each pool.
:::

## Doubled haploid (DH) lines

```{r}
#| label: g-dh
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.4
diagrama(
  data.table(id = c("C", "Fu", "F1", "H", "DH"),
             x = c(0, 0, 3.6, 7.6, 11.6), y = c(0.9, -0.9, 0, 0, 0),
             rotulo = c("Central", "Founder", "F1", "Haploid\n(n)",
                        "DH (2n)\nhomozygous"),
             cor = c("grey92", "grey92", "grey60", "grey60", "#1F3A5F")),
  data.table(de = c("C", "Fu", "F1", "H"), para = c("F1", "F1", "H", "DH"),
             rotulo = c("", "", "haploid\ninducer", "colchicine"),
             lx = c(NA, NA, 5.6, 9.6), ly = c(NA, NA, 0.95, 0.95)),
  largura = 2.4, altura = 1.3, tamanho = 6.5, tamanho_rotulo = 5.5)
```

::: destaque
One meiosis · 50% central + 50% founder
:::

::: notes
The F1 plant is pollinated by a haploid inducer; the chromosomes of the
haploid embryos are doubled with colchicine. Result: fully homozygous lines in
a single generation. Since there was only one meiosis (in the F1), each DH is
a mosaic of large blocks from the central line and the founder. This will show
up in LD and in STRUCTURE.
:::

## The data

```{r}
#| label: g-numeros
#| fig-height: 4
numeros(c("2,290", "24", "23", "56,110"),
        c("genotyped\nlines", "DH\nfamilies", "parents",
          "SNPs\n(50K chip)"))
```

GEO **GSE50558** · Bauer et al. 2013 · Lehermeier et al. 2014

::: notes
The GEO matrix contains both pools together. Lehermeier et al. (2014)
analysed the dent and flint panels separately and also jointly (34,116 SNPs
in the joint analysis); we do the same: a "global" dataset (dent + flint)
and one dataset per pool. Lehermeier used 10 dent and 11 flint families; the
GEO has 3 more (CFD01, CFF01, CFF02), the crosses between pools, which we use
as controls.
:::

# From SNPs to clean data

## The chip reads two alleles: A and B

```{r}
#| label: g-codigos
#| fig-height: 5.8
cod <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "codigos_genotipo.tsv"))
cod[, codigo := factor(codigo, c("AA", "BB", "AB", "NC"),
                       c("AA", "BB", "AB", "no call"))]
cod[, tipo := factor(tipo, c("Parental", "DH"), c("Parents", "DH"))]
ggplot(cod, aes(codigo, prop, fill = codigo == "AB")) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(prop, 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 7) +
  facet_wrap(~ tipo) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey60", `TRUE` = "#B22222"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.55)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

::: destaque
DH almost without AB → heterozygote = error → missing data
:::

::: notes
SNP = a genome position with two alleles. The Illumina chip calls AA, AB or
BB. DH lines and inbred parents should be 100% homozygous; the little AB that
shows up (0.3% in the DH) is a calling error or residual heterozygosity. That
is why we treat AB as missing data.
:::

## PLINK: the Swiss army knife for SNPs

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- file formats
- filters (QC)
- LD and pruning
- PCA, F~ST~
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Built for **humans**: 22 autosomes + X, Y

**Maize**: 10 chromosomes, no sex chromosomes

```r
c("--chr-set", "10", "no-xy")
```
:::
::::

::: notes
PLINK is the standard program for handling SNP data, and we use it for all
the filtering steps that follow. By default it assumes the human genome and
would treat chromosomes differently (for example, sex chromosomes).
--chr-set 10 no-xy says there are 10 autosomes and no sex chromosomes. We
call PLINK from R with system2(), in the rodar_plink() function, so the whole
workflow lives in a single script.
:::

## SNPs have errors: filtering

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: g-funil
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
funil <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "funil_cq.tsv"))[1:5]
funil[, etapa := c("SNP chip", "With position", "GenTrain ≥ 0.7",
                   "Call rate ≥ 90%", "MAF ≥ 1%")]
funil[, etapa := factor(etapa, rev(etapa))]
funil[, removidos := shift(snps) - snps]
ggplot(funil, aes(snps, etapa)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1F3A5F", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(snps, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)), hjust = 1.1,
            colour = "white", size = 7, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(is.na(removidos), "",
                               paste0("− ", format(removidos, big.mark = ",",
                                                   trim = TRUE)))),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 6, colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.35)), breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```r
rodar_plink(
  "--bfile", "cornfed_bruto",
  "--exclude",
    "gentrain_baixo.txt",
  "--remove",
    "dh_faltantes.txt",
  "--geno", "0.1",
  "--maf",  "0.01",
  "--make-bed",
  "--out", "cornfed_cq")
```

```
33430 variants and
2269 samples pass
```
:::
::::

::: notes
GenTrain: a quality score for how well the chip intensities cluster (SNPs
scoring < 0.7 have unreliable calls; they are listed in gentrain_baixo.txt
and removed with --exclude). Call rate (--geno 0.1): a SNP missing in more
than 10% of the samples is removed. MAF (--maf 0.01): an almost monomorphic
SNP says nothing about structure and is more error-prone. We also removed 21
DH lines with more than 10% missing data (--remove). Same criteria as
Lehermeier et al. 2014 (they kept 34,116 SNPs; we kept 33,430).
:::

## MAF: minor allele frequency

```{r}
#| label: g-maf
#| fig-height: 6
maf <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "maf.tsv.gz"))
maf[, conjunto := factor(conjunto, c("global", "dent", "flint"),
                         c("global (dent + flint)", "dent", "flint"))]
mono <- maf[, .(n = sum(maf == 0, na.rm = TRUE)), by = conjunto]
ggplot(maf, aes(maf, fill = conjunto)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 0.5, 0.025), colour = "white") +
  geom_text(data = mono[n > 0],
            aes(x = 0.25, y = Inf, label = paste(format(n, big.mark = ","),
                                                 "fixed SNPs")),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 7, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ conjunto) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey40", cor_pool[["Dent"]],
                               cor_pool[["Flint"]]) |>
                      setNames(levels(maf$conjunto)), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "MAF", y = "SNPs")
```

::: destaque
Filters recomputed within each dataset
:::

::: notes
MAF = frequency of the less common allele. A SNP that separates dent from
flint is common overall but may be fixed within a pool (almost 2,000 in dent
and 2,600 in flint). That is why MAF and call rate were recomputed in each
dataset analysed. "Global" is the combined dataset with both pools, as in
Lehermeier's joint analysis.
:::

## Linkage disequilibrium (LD)

```{r}
#| label: g-ld
#| fig-height: 6.2
ld <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "ld_decaimento.tsv"))
ld[, grupo := factor(grupo, c("DH dent", "DH flint", "Parentais"),
                     c("DH dent", "DH flint", "Parents"))]
ggplot(ld[distancia_mb <= 10], aes(distancia_mb, r2, colour = grupo)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.2, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = 0.215, label = "pruning threshold (r² = 0.2)",
           hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 7) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`DH dent` = cor_pool[["Dent"]],
                                 `DH flint` = cor_pool[["Flint"]],
                                 Parents = "grey40"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "distance between SNPs (Mb)", y = "mean r²")
```

::: notes
LD = association between alleles at nearby loci: they are inherited together.
r² measures it (0 = independent, 1 = always together). In the DH lines LD is
higher and decays slowly with distance, because there was a single meiosis.
STRUCTURE assumes independent loci within each group; SNPs in LD repeat the
same information many times and make the result overconfident.
:::

## LD pruning

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: g-poda
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
# SNPs que entraram no STRUCTURE no cluster (todas as amostras)
plano <- unique(fread(file.path(dir_prod, "evanno.tsv"))[
  , .(etapa = conjunto, snps = loci)])
poda <- rbind(fread(file.path(dir_comp, "funil_cq.tsv"))[5, .(etapa, snps)],
              plano)
rotulos_poda <- c("after\nfilters", "global\n(dent + flint)", "dent", "flint")
poda[, etapa := factor(rotulos_poda[
  match(etapa, c("MAF ≥ 1%", "global", "dent", "flint"))], rotulos_poda)]
ggplot(poda, aes(etapa, snps, fill = etapa)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(snps, big.mark = ",")), vjust = -0.3, size = 8,
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1F3A5F", "grey40", cor_pool[["Dent"]],
                               cor_pool[["Flint"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, expand = expansion(c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```
:::

```r
# window 50, step 5,
# r² > 0.2 → one goes
rodar_plink(
  "--bfile", "cornfed_cq",
  "--keep",  "dent.txt",
  "--maf",   "0.01",
  "--geno",  "0.1",
  "--indep-pairwise",
    "50", "5", "0.2",
  "--out",   "dent")
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Pruning slides along the genome in 50-SNP windows (step of 5). Within the
window, for each pair with r² > 0.2, one SNP is removed. It is done
separately in each dataset (global, dent, flint), always starting from the
same 33,430 SNPs, so the three lists are mostly different SNPs and do not add
up. Fewer SNPs remain within the pools because many SNPs become fixed there
and because LD is stronger: all DH lines in a pool share the same central
line. Bonus: STRUCTURE runs much faster.
:::

# STRUCTURE

## The idea of the model

```{r}
#| label: g-modelo
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
diagrama(
  data.table(id = c("G1", "G2", "I"), x = c(0, 0, 5), y = c(1, -1, 0),
             rotulo = c("Group 1\nfrequencies p1", "Group 2\nfrequencies p2",
                        "Individual\nQ = 0.7 | 0.3"),
             cor = c(cores[["Cluster2"]], cores[["Cluster1"]], "grey35")),
  data.table(de = c("G1", "G2"), para = c("I", "I"),
             rotulo = c("70%", "30%"),
             lx = c(2.5, 2.5), ly = c(1.05, -1.05)),
  largura = 3.2, altura = 1.3, tamanho_rotulo = 7)
```

::: destaque
K groups in Hardy-Weinberg · Q = fraction from each group
:::

::: notes
STRUCTURE (Pritchard et al. 2000) assumes there are K ancestral populations,
each with its own allele frequencies, in Hardy-Weinberg and linkage
equilibrium. It looks for the partition of individuals (or of parts of their
genomes, in the admixture model) that brings each group as close as possible
to that equilibrium. It estimates the allele frequencies of each group (P)
and the proportions of each individual (Q) at the same time. In the example,
70% of the individual's genome comes from group 1 and 30% from group 2.
:::

## What STRUCTURE reads

```r
rodar_plink("--bfile", "cornfed_cq", "--keep", "dent.txt",
            "--extract", "dent.prune.in",
            "--recode", "structure", "--out", "dent")
```

```
PZE-101000088 PZE-101000209 PZE-101000451 ...   ← SNP names
-1 157033 604385 ...                            ← map distances (bp)
F353      1  2 2  2 2  2 2  2 2 ...
UH007     1  2 2  2 2  2 2  2 2 ...
CFD06-002 7  0 0  1 1  0 0  2 2 ...             ← 0 0 = missing
CFF15-141 25 2 2  2 2  1 1  2 2 ...
```

::: destaque
One row per line · family code · 2 columns per SNP (alleles 1/2)
:::

::: notes
PLINK exports the pruned SNPs in STRUCTURE's format (--recode structure).
Row 1: SNP names. Row 2: distance to the previous SNP on the same chromosome
(-1 = first SNP of a chromosome). Then one row per individual: its name, a
number for its family (not used by the model; USEPOPINFO = 0), and two
columns per SNP, one for each allele copy (1 or 2; 0 = missing). DH lines
are homozygous, so the two columns are always equal (1 1 or 2 2). The global
file has 2,269 rows of individuals and 2,226 SNPs, i.e. 4,454 columns.
:::

## Parameters

| Parameter | Exploration | Cluster | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| samples | 743 | 2,269 | |
| K | 1–6 · 1–12 · 1–14 | 1–8 · 1–13 · 1–14 | groups tested |
| replicates | 3 | 5 | same answer? |
| BURNIN | 10,000 | 50,000 | discarded |
| NUMREPS | 20,000 | 100,000 | used |
| NOADMIX, FREQSCORR | 0, 1 | 0, 1 | model |
| RANDOMIZE | 0 + `-D` | 0 + `-D` | reproducible |

::: notes
Two stages: a quick local exploration (subsample, short chains) to choose the
K ranges, and the final analysis on the cluster with all samples and chains
five times longer. From here on, the results shown are the cluster's.
Admixture model with correlated allele frequencies, as in Caniato et al.
2011. K goes beyond the expected number of groups (dent has 11 families; we
tested up to 13). Watch out: with RANDOMIZE 1 (the default) STRUCTURE ignores
the seed. Another detail: in the parameter file, 100000 must not become
1e+05, which STRUCTURE would read as 1.
:::

## MCMC: burn-in and convergence

```{r}
#| label: g-traco
#| fig-height: 6.2
tracos <- fread(file.path(dir_prod, "tracos.tsv.gz"))
traco <- function(conj, k) {
  tracos[conjunto == conj & K == k & fase == "amostragem"][
    , rep := paste("replicate", rep)]
}
graf_traco <- function(d, titulo, destaque_r1) {
  ggplot(d, aes(iteracao / 1000, lnlike / 1000, colour = rep)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(if (destaque_r1) "#B22222" else "grey20",
                                   "grey35", "grey50", "grey65", "grey80"),
                        name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "iteration (thousands)", y = "ln likelihood (thousands)",
         title = titulo) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}
graf_traco(traco("flint", 14), "flint, K = 14", TRUE) +
  graf_traco(traco("global", 4), "global, K = 4", FALSE)
```

::: destaque
Jump → unstable replicate · different plateaus → several solutions
:::

::: notes
STRUCTURE runs a Markov chain (MCMC): it starts at a random point and keeps
improving. The burn-in (50,000 iterations) is discarded; the plot shows the
following 100,000. Two different problems:
(1) On the left, replicate 1 of flint K = 14 jumps to another plateau around
iteration 97,000: the chain had not stabilised yet. Its variance of the ln
likelihood is much larger than the others' (criterion: > 3× the median of the
replicates of the same K). It was the only unstable replicate out of 169; it
is left out.
(2) On the right, the five replicates of global K = 4 are stable, but each on
its own plateau: each chain found a different solution. This is not a bug; it
shows that with 4 groups there are several almost equally good partitions.
:::

## Running it: from laptop to cluster

```r
# local: several runs in parallel, 1 core each
parallel::mclapply(1:96, rodar_structure, mc.cores = 10)
```

```bash
# UFV cluster (PBS): one job per dataset × K × replicate
qsub -N "$nome" -l walltime="$walltime" \
     -v CONJ=$conj,K=$k,REP=$rep,SEMENTE=$semente \
     structure_job.pbs
```

::: destaque
Local: 96 runs in 6.5 h · Cluster: 169 of 175 jobs
:::

::: notes
Each STRUCTURE run uses a single core. Locally we ran 10 at a time with
mclapply (exploration, 6.5 hours). On the UFV cluster, each run becomes a PBS
job. Finishing everything would take about 14 days on the cluster, so we used
what was ready: dent and flint complete (65 and 70 runs) and global with 34 of
40 (2 replicates of K = 6 and 4 of K = 7 are missing). We checked the cluster
input files and parameters: they are identical to those produced by our
script.
:::

## The output: the Q matrix

```{r}
#| label: t-q
exemplo <- q_medio[conjunto == "global" & K == 2 &
                     id %in% c("B73", "UH007", "CFD03-008", "CFF09-010",
                               "CFD01-021")]
if (exemplo[, uniqueN(id)] < 5) {
  # se algum desses ids não existir, pega o primeiro de cada família
  ids <- q_medio[conjunto == "global" & K == 2 &
                   familia %in% c("CFD03", "CFF09", "CFD01"), id[1], by = familia]$V1
  exemplo <- q_medio[conjunto == "global" & K == 2 &
                       id %in% c("B73", "UH007", ids)]
}
tab <- dcast(exemplo, id + familia ~ grupo, value.var = "fracao")
tab[familia == "Parental", familia := "parent"]
setnames(tab, c("individual", "family", "Q group 1", "Q group 2"))
tab[, `:=`(`Q group 1` = round(`Q group 1`, 2), `Q group 2` = round(`Q group 2`, 2))]
knitr::kable(tab, align = "llcc")
```

::: destaque
One row per individual · sum = 1
:::

## How to read the plot

```{r}
#| label: g-como-ler
#| fig-height: 5.8
ex <- data.table(ind = factor(1:6),
                 g1 = c(1, 1, 0.5, 0.7, 0, 0))
ex <- melt(ex[, g2 := 1 - g1], id.vars = "ind", variable.name = "grupo",
           value.name = "q")
rotulos <- data.table(ind = factor(c(1.5, 3, 4, 5.5)), x = c(1.5, 3, 4, 5.5),
                      texto = c("pure\ngroup 1", "50 / 50", "70 / 30",
                                "pure\ngroup 2"))
ggplot(ex, aes(ind, q, fill = grupo)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.97) +
  geom_text(data = rotulos, aes(x = x, y = 1.12, label = texto),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, lineheight = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(cores[2:1]), labels = c("group 1", "group 2"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1"),
                     limits = c(0, 1.25)) +
  labs(x = "individuals", y = "Q") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

::: destaque
One bar = one individual · colours = fraction of the genome
:::

::: notes
Each row of the Q matrix becomes one bar: the height of each colour is the
fraction of that individual's genome assigned to each group.
:::

# R: tying it all together

## One workflow, one script

```{r}
#| label: g-fluxo
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 2.6
diagrama(
  data.table(id = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), x = c(0, 3.4, 6.8, 10.2), y = 0,
             rotulo = c("R\nreads GEO", "PLINK\nfilters, LD",
                        "STRUCTURE\nK = 1 ... 14", "R + pophelper\nΔK, plots"),
             cor = c("#1F3A5F", "grey45", "#B22222", "#1F3A5F")),
  data.table(de = c("A", "B", "C"), para = c("B", "C", "D")),
  largura = 2.7, altura = 1.3, tamanho = 7)
```

```r
q  <- readQ(arquivos_f)              # read the Q matrices
ev <- evannoMethodStructure(
        summariseQ(tabulateQ(q)))    # Evanno's ΔK
q  <- alignK(q, type = "within")     # align the replicates
```

::: notes
R reads the GEO data (data.table), calls PLINK and STRUCTURE, and analyses
the results with the pophelper package. One detail: STRUCTURE's groups have
no names, and "group 1" in one replicate may be "group 3" in another. That is
why we align the replicates before averaging them.
:::

# Results

## How many groups? Evanno's ΔK

```{r}
#| label: g-evanno
#| fig-height: 6.4
ev <- fread(file.path(dir_prod, "evanno.tsv"))
ev[, conjunto := factor(conjunto, c("global", "dent", "flint"))]
p1 <- ggplot(ev, aes(k, elpdmean / 1e3)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ conjunto, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = function(l) seq(1, floor(l[2]), 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "ln P(D|K)\n(thousands)")
p2 <- ggplot(ev[!is.na(deltaK)], aes(k, deltaK)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#B22222") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#B22222") +
  facet_wrap(~ conjunto, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = function(l) seq(1, floor(l[2]), 2)) +
  labs(x = "K", y = "ΔK") +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank())
p1 / p2
```

::: destaque
ΔK: K = 2 (global, flint) · K = 3 (dent)
:::

::: notes
ln P(D|K) always rises with K: more groups always explain the data a bit
better. Evanno et al. 2005 proposed looking at where that rise changes pace:
ΔK is the second derivative divided by the standard deviation across
replicates. In global (ΔK = 49,000 at K = 2) and flint (3,900 at K = 2) the
peak is clear. In dent, ΔK is low for every K (maximum 11, at K = 3, and 7 at
K = 2): the dent replicates already disagree at K = 2 (next slide). ΔK tends
to point to the top level of the hierarchy, which is why we also look at the
bar plots. In global, K = 7 has a single replicate and therefore no ΔK.
:::

## Do the replicates agree?

```{r}
#| label: g-modos
#| fig-height: 5.8
modos <- fread(file.path(dir_prod, "modos.tsv"))
modos[, conjunto := factor(conjunto, c("global", "dent", "flint"))]
# K com menos de 5 réplicas prontas (global K = 6 e 7, flint K = 14 sem a
# instável) ficam em cinza: a proporção ali vale menos
modos[, completo := replicas == 5]
ggplot(modos[K > 1], aes(K, no_modo_principal / replicas, fill = completo)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = no_modo_principal), vjust = -0.3, size = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1F3A5F", `FALSE` = "grey70"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "5 replicates", `FALSE` = "fewer than 5"),
                    name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ conjunto, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = function(l) seq(2, floor(l[2]), 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.12),
                     breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "K", y = "replicates with\nthe same solution")
```

::: destaque
Only low K values are reproducible
:::

::: notes
For each K, we compare the replicates with the one with the highest
ln P(D|K): two replicates have "the same solution" when, on average, they
assign more than 90% of each individual's genome to the same groups. The
number above each bar is how many replicates share that solution; in grey,
the K values with fewer than 5 finished replicates (in global, K = 7 has only
one, so its "100%" means nothing). In global and flint, all replicates agree
up to K = 3. In dent, only 3 of 5 agree already at K = 2. Above that, almost
every replicate has its own solution. Practical consequence: the high-K plots
show the solution with the highest ln P(D|K), one among several; their
details should not be taken literally.
:::

## Global, K = 2: dent × flint

```{r}
#| label: g-global-k2
#| fig-height: 4.8
barras("global", 2)
```

::: destaque
CFD01, CFF01, CFF02: ~60/40, their parents come from both pools
:::

::: notes
Each column is a family (all DH lines; the width is the number of lines). The
red group gathers the dent families and the blue one the flint families. The
three control families appear admixed, as expected from the pedigree: CFD01
0.62/0.38, CFF01 0.60/0.40 and CFF02 0.63/0.37 (close to 60/40, not 50/50).
Some flint families (CFF04, 05, 06, 10) have some red: their founders are not
as "flint" as the central line UH007.
:::

## Within the Dent pool

```{r}
#| label: g-dent
#| fig-height: 6
barras("dent", c(2, 3, 4, 6))
```

::: destaque
D11 = F353 × UH304: both Iodent, the most similar pair (SM = 0.77)
:::

::: notes
K = 2: blue = the central line F353's group, red = founders. CFD11 is all
blue, and CFD03, 04 and 10 almost all blue, because their founders (UH304,
D06, D09, UH250) resemble F353.
Why is D11 all green at K = 3? CFD11 comes from F353 × UH304, and both lines
share an Iodent background. In Lehermeier et al. (2014, Table 1) this is the
most similar parent pair in the dent panel (simple matching = 0.765, against
0.61–0.67 for the others). Its DH lines are therefore very alike and form a
large, homogeneous block, which STRUCTURE gives its own group (green),
together with F353 and UH304 themselves.
From K = 4 onwards, families split off one by one (CFD06, CFD07...). Note:
in dent the replicates already disagree at K = 2 (3 of 5), and from K = 5 on
each replicate has its own solution.
:::

## Within the Flint pool

```{r}
#| label: g-flint
#| fig-height: 6
barras("flint", c(2, 3, 4, 6))
```

::: destaque
F12, F13: founders closest to UH007 (SM = 0.79 and 0.82)
:::

::: notes
K = 2: blue = the central line UH007's group. Why are F12 and F13 blue? Their
founders, UH006 (CFF12) and UH009 (CFF13), are the most similar to UH007 in
the flint panel (simple matching = 0.791 and 0.815; Lehermeier et al. 2014,
Table 1), so both families look like the central line.
Why does F13 turn orange at K = 4? With 4 groups, STRUCTURE splits that
"central-like" block in two: orange = UH007, UH009 and CFF13; blue = UH006
and CFF12. K = 3 (green): the families whose founders are more distant from
the central line, including CFF01 (F353, the dent central line) and CFF02
(B73, dent). Up to K = 3 the 5 replicates agree; at K = 4, 3 of 5.
:::

## PCA: another view

```{r}
#| label: g-pca
#| fig-height: 6.6
pca <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "pca.eigenvec"))
pca <- merge(pca, amostras[, .(IID = id, tipo, pool, familia)], by = "IID")
# DH: cor pelo pool; as três famílias com pais dos dois pools em laranja
mistas <- "CFD01 · CFF01 · CFF02 (both pools)"
pca[tipo == "DH", grupo_cor := fifelse(familia %in% c("CFD01", "CFF01", "CFF02"),
                                       mistas, paste("DH", pool))]
pca[, grupo_cor := factor(grupo_cor, c("DH Dent", "DH Flint", mistas))]
ggplot(pca, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(data = pca[tipo == "DH" & grupo_cor != mistas],
             aes(colour = grupo_cor), size = 2, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = pca[grupo_cor == mistas], aes(colour = grupo_cor),
             size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = pca[tipo == "Parental"], aes(fill = pool), shape = 21,
             size = 6, colour = "black") +
  geom_text_repel(data = pca[tipo == "Parental"], aes(label = IID), size = 6,
                  max.overlaps = 30, seed = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(cor_pool, "#FF7F00"),
                                        c("DH Dent", "DH Flint", mistas)),
                      name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cor_pool, guide = "none") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 6, alpha = 1))) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

::: notes
PCA assumes no genetic model at all: it summarises SNP variation in a few
axes. PC1 separates dent and flint, like STRUCTURE's K = 2. The orange points
(the three families with parents from both pools: CFD01, CFF01, CFF02) lie
in between. The DH lines form "clouds" around the midpoint between the
central line and their founder. The large circles with names are the
parents. All 2,269 samples, with the 2,255 SNPs pruned for the global
dataset.
:::

# F-statistics

## Wahlund effect

```{r}
#| label: g-wahlund
#| fig-height: 5.6
w <- data.table(
  grupo = factor(c("Subpop. 1\np = 0.8", "Subpop. 2\np = 0.2", "Pooled\np̄ = 0.5"),
                 c("Subpop. 1\np = 0.8", "Subpop. 2\np = 0.2", "Pooled\np̄ = 0.5")),
  H = c(0.32, 0.32, 0.5),
  tipo = c("H_S", "H_S", "H_T"))
ggplot(w, aes(grupo, H, fill = tipo)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.32, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(H)), vjust = -0.3, size = 9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(H_S = "grey55", H_T = "#1F3A5F"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.6), breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "expected\nheterozygosity 2pq")
```

::: destaque
Pooling subpopulations → "missing" heterozygotes
:::

::: notes
Each subpopulation in Hardy-Weinberg has 2pq = 0.32 heterozygotes. If we pool
the two and compute with the mean frequency (0.5), we would expect 0.5. But
the actual heterozygotes are still 0.32. This deficit, caused only by the
subdivision, is the Wahlund effect. F_ST measures exactly this:
1 − H_S/H_T = 1 − 0.32/0.5 = 0.36.
:::

## Wright's F: three levels

$$
\underbrace{F_{IS} = 1 - \frac{H_O}{H_S}}_{\text{within}} \qquad
\underbrace{F_{ST} = 1 - \frac{H_S}{H_T}}_{\text{between}} \qquad
\underbrace{F_{IT} = 1 - \frac{H_O}{H_T}}_{\text{total}}
$$

<br>

$$
(1 - F_{IT}) = (1 - F_{IS})\,(1 - F_{ST})
$$

::: notes
H_O: observed heterozygosity (fraction of AB). H_S: expected under
Hardy-Weinberg within each subpopulation, averaged across them. H_T: expected
in the total, using the mean frequency. F_IS measures inbreeding within
subpopulations, F_ST the differentiation among them and F_IT the total
inbreeding.
:::

## F in the CornFed data

```{r}
#| label: t-f
f <- fread(file.path(dir_comp, "estatisticas_f.tsv"))
f[, nivel := c(`Pools (dent x flint)` = "Pools (dent × flint)",
               `Famílias dent` = "Dent families",
               `Famílias flint` = "Flint families")[nivel]]
f <- f[, .(nivel, H_O, H_S, H_T, F_IS, F_ST, F_IT)]
num <- names(f)[-1]
f[, (num) := lapply(.SD, function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)),
  .SDcols = num]
knitr::kable(f, align = "lcccccc",
             col.names = c("subpopulations", "H~O~", "H~S~", "H~T~",
                           "F~IS~", "F~ST~", "F~IT~"))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
F~IS~ ≈ 1: DH lines are homozygous
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
F~ST~ families **>** F~ST~ pools
:::
::::

::: notes
F_IS ≈ 1 is no surprise: DH lines are 100% homozygous by construction
(H_O ≈ 0.001). The interesting part is F_ST. Between dent and flint it is
0.20 (PLINK, with the Weir & Cockerham estimator, gives 0.22). Among families
within a pool it is higher, ~0.35: the families differ more from each other
than the two heterotic pools do. Why? F_ST is the share of the total
diversity that lies between groups. Each pool is very diverse inside (many
founders, H_S = 0.25), so only ~20% of the diversity is between pools. Each
family comes from a cross of just two inbred parents, so it is very uniform
inside (H_S = 0.16–0.19), and most of the diversity lies between families.
:::

# Take-home

## What STRUCTURE found

1. **K = 2**: dent × flint, the historical split
2. Within a pool: **central line** × founders
3. Beyond that: **families**, i.e. the pedigree
4. In a breeder-built population, **there is no "true K"**

::: destaque
Structure ≠ only natural populations: relatedness is structure too
:::

::: notes
The question of this work was: what does STRUCTURE detect when the
"population" was built by breeders? Answer: at the top level, the split
between heterotic groups; below it, the relatedness structure of the
families. F_ST among families being higher than between pools reinforces
this. Limitations: global is missing 6 of its 40 runs (K = 6 and 7), and
above K ≈ 3 the replicates do not reach the same solution, so only low K
values are firm conclusions.
:::
